paper_title: VascuSR: Iterative Anatomy-Aware Diffusion for CT Super-Resolution

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generative super-resolution (SR) can recover sharp detail in computed tomography (CT) images from severely downsampled observations, but the missing high-frequency content is not uniquely determined by the low-resolution input. Consequently, visually plausible reconstructions may contain anatomically unsupported vascular detail, such as missing, spurious, or incorrectly connected vessels. To overcome this challenge, we introduce VascuSR, an iterative anatomy-aware diffusion framework that combines image reconstruction with explicit 3D vascular guidance. First, to provide richer anatomical guidance, we use an explicit 3D vascular representation that captures structural information beyond individual slices. This representation also simplifies vascular refinement by allowing a lightweight 3D generative refiner to focus on vascular structure rather than complex CT appearance. Second, to guide slice-wise SR, a lightweight anatomy controller injects the refined structure into the diffusion decoder, while iterative feedback updates this guidance from each new SR volume. On re-annotated MSD Task08 and HVM datasets, VascuSR outperforms interpolation and learning-based SR baselines in segmentation accuracy (Dice and clDice) and 3D vascular structure (connectivity and mean centerline distance), while maintaining image quality comparable to its SR backbone. Compared with learning-based baselines, VascuSR reduces class-averaged connected-component counts by over 20% on both datasets and mean centerline distance by over 10% on MSD.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Medical image super-resolution (SR) aims to recover image detail from low-resolution observations while preserving anatomically meaningful structure. This is particularly challenging for contrastenhanced vascular CT, where vessels are thin, highly branched, and span wide range of diameters and curvatures: small peripheral branches may additionally exhibit weak contrast against surrounding tissue (Lesage et al., 2009). At high upsampling factors, much of this fine image detail is poorly determined by the observed low-resolution image, making the reconstruction inherently ambiguous (Ledig et al., 2017). Recent deep SR has progressed from deterministic regression to generative reconstruction, enabling sharper and more realistic image detail (Zhang et al., 2018b; Liang et al., 2021; Ledig et al., 2017; Saharia et al., 2023; Yue et al., 2023). However, visual plausibility does not guarantee anatomical fidelity. Errors that are small in image space can be structurally significant: short discontinuity may disconnect an otherwise continuous vessel tree, while spurious connection may alter its branching structure. Such failures are not well characterized by conventional image-quality metrics. High SSIM, for example, can coexist with hallucinated anatomical structures in medical reconstruction (Muckley et al., 2021), and improved image-quality metrics do not necessarily translate to better downstream detection performance (Li et al., 2021). Deep-learning-based CT reconstruction may also blur or remove small vessels despite producing visually high-quality images (Koetzier et al., 2023). For tubular structures in particular, voxel-wise overlap alone does not fully characterize topological correctness, motivating connectivity-aware measures such as clDice (Shit et al., 2021). reconstructed CT image can therefore appear locally plausible while still containing broken, missing, Equal contribution. Jiahe Huang <chh118@ucsd.edu> and Rose Yu <roseyu@ucsd.edu>. Work partially done at the University of California, San Diego. Correspondence to: 1 Preprint Figure 1: Overview of VascuSR. Starting from an initial SR estimate, the recovered HV/PV anatomy is refined in three dimensions and fed back through lightweight anatomy controller to condition the next diffusion-based reconstruction. Repeating this process for feedback rounds progressively couples image super-resolution with volumetric vascular refinement. or incorrectly connected vessels. These challenges motivate explicitly incorporating volumetric vascular structure into the reconstruction process, rather than relying on image appearance alone. To address these limitations, we propose VascuSR, an iterative anatomy-aware diffusion framework for CT SR that targets both image fidelity and vascular anatomical plausibility. Rather than relying only on individual 2D slices, VascuSR represents vascular anatomy explicitly in 3D. This representation provides richer information about vascular topology while separating vascular structure from CT intensity and organ texture, making anatomical refinement simpler learning task. We therefore use conditional 3D rectified flow to refine the vascular representation. lightweight multi-scale anatomy controller then transforms the refined representation into conditioning features for the diffusion decoder. At each round, the vascular representation is re-extracted and refined from the latest SR volume to guide the next reconstruction, so that the anatomical condition and SR output are updated in turn through the feedback loop. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce explicit 3D vascular representations as anatomical guidance for slice-wise CT super-resolution. Separating vascular refinement from image reconstruction simplifies structural learning while retaining HR supervision for image fidelity. We develop an iterative refinementconditioning mechanism that combines conditional 3D rectified-flow vascular refiner with lightweight multi-scale anatomy controller, allowing anatomical guidance to adapt to each updated SR volume. We evaluate VascuSR on two public vascular CT datasets across image quality, vascular overlap, and three-dimensional vascular structure. VascuSR reduces class-averaged component counts by over 20% on both datasets and class-averaged MCD by over 10% on MSD, while comparisons with direct joint optimization support the benefits of the decoupled design.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: 2.1 SUPER-RESOLUTION AND GENERATIVE INVERSE PROBLEMS Super-resolution can be formulated as an ill-posed inverse problem, where high-resolution signal must be recovered from degraded low-resolution observation (Wang et al., 2021). Because multiple 2 Preprint HR solutions may be consistent with the same LR input, successful reconstruction requires appropriate priors over the missing fine-scale structure. Deterministic SR methods learn such priors implicitly from paired training data through direct LR-to-HR mapping, using convolutional architectures such as SRCNN, EDSR, and RCAN (Dong et al., 2014; Lim et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018b), or Transformer-based models such as SwinIR and HAT (Liang et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2023). These approaches achieve strong distortion-oriented performance, but training with pixel-wise objectives can produce overly smooth reconstructions. Generative methods instead model distribution over plausible HR solutions. Adversarial approaches such as SRGAN use perceptual and adversarial objectives to recover sharper image detail (Ledig et al., 2017), while diffusion models provide probabilistic reconstruction framework through iterative denoising. SR3 conditions the reverse diffusion process on the LR observation, whereas ResShift constructs residual-shifting trajectory between LR and HR representations for more efficient sampling (Saharia et al., 2023; Yue et al., 2023). StableSR and DiffBIR further exploit pretrained latent diffusion models as generative priors for image restoration (Wang et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2024). More broadly, this coarse-to-fine inverse formulation is common across AI for Science, including medical imaging and physical-system reconstruction, where generative priors are often combined with domain-specific constraints to restrict the space of plausible solutions (Chung et al., 2023a; Huang et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2026). 2.2 ANATOMYAND TASK-AWARE MEDICAL SUPER-RESOLUTION Medical SR methods incorporate domain knowledge primarily through either observation consistency or anatomyand task-specific priors. One line of work enforces consistency between the reconstruction and the LR input in the image or measurement domain. Chung et al. (2023b) reuse score model trained for MR denoising for post-hoc SR, alternating reverse-diffusion steps with image-level data-consistency updates. GAN-CIRCLE regularizes bidirectional LR-HR mappings through cycle consistency (You et al., 2020), CMISR iteratively corrects re-reconstruction errors (Li et al., 2024b), and DynamicDPS applies adaptive diffusion posterior guidance to low-field MRI enhancement (Kim et al., 2025). Such constraints improve agreement with the observed image or measurement. However, this agreement alone does not ensure faithful recovery of fine anatomical structures that are poorly resolved in the input. complementary line incorporates structural or task-specific information. DiffMSR performs diffusion in compact latent space to generate high-frequency-detail prior for multi-contrast MRI SR (Li et al., 2024a), while DSDM combines image and structure streams with Hessian-derived vesseland blob-sensitive priors for CT SR (Chu et al., 2023). The dual-guidance SR network of Chi et al. (2023) combines segmentation-derived ROI guidance with inter-slice information for CT superresolution. However, an important gap remains in how structural guidance can improve vascular anatomical fidelity, and how this fidelity should be assessed beyond conventional image-quality metrics.

As illustrated in Figure 1, VascuSR combines slice-wise diffusion SR backbone, 3D vascular refiner, and an anatomy controller. The backbone reconstructs high-resolution CT images, the refiner improves 3D vascular structure, and the controller injects the refined anatomy into the diffusion decoder. The backbone and controller are trained jointly with HR supervision, while the refiner learns vascular correction separately in the 3D vascular representation space, decoupling structural refinement from CT intensity reconstruction. During inference, the vascular representation extracted from the current SR volume is refined and passed through the controller to guide the next reconstruction, forming an iterative feedback loop in which the anatomical condition is updated after each SR pass. sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS
sections.content: 4.1 DATASETS We use two publicly available contrast-enhanced CT datasets for 8 SR, pairing each 512 512 HR slice with 64 64 LR input. All methods use identical preprocessing within each dataset, and all splits and analyses are patient-level to avoid leakage between correlated slices. No patient in the reported test sets is used to train the SR models, VSNet, or FlowSeg3D (the vascular refiner). Patient splits and additional implementation details are provided in Appendix A.1. Re-annotated MSD Task08 HepaticVessel. The official Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) Task08 dataset comprises 443 CT volumes: 303 labeled training volumes and 140 challenge-test volumes whose annotations are not publicly released (Antonelli et al., 2022). VSNet re-annotates the 303 training volumes with separate HV and PV masks. HVM. The public Hepatic Vessel Map (HVM) dataset (Xie et al., 2026) contains 282 dual-center portal-venous-phase contrast-enhanced CT volumes with separate HV and PV annotations. We exclude one case with an incomplete imagelabel pair, leaving 281 complete CTHVPV triplets. Because the released volumes fall into three stored-intensity domains and are not uniformly raw-HU CT, we clip all volumes to their shared range [40, 160] before normalization. 4.2 BASELINES We compare VascuSR with four groups of baselines: Interpolation. Bicubic interpolation provides non-learned reference, reconstructing HR images without learned image or anatomical priors. Deterministic SR. RCAN (Zhang et al., 2018b), SwinIR (Liang et al., 2021), and HAT (Chen et al., 2023) represent convolutional and Transformer-based reconstruction methods. Diffusion SR. ResShift (Yue et al., 2023) performs SR through residual-shifting diffusion and serves as the backbone of VascuSR. Joint image and anatomical optimization. Extends ResShift by adding Dice and softclDice losses, computed through frozen VSNet segmenter, to its image reconstruction objective during fine-tuning. Details are provided in Appendix B. Learned baselines are trained or fine-tuned on the same LRHR training pairs within each dataset. We use each methods official training recipe as starting point and select hyperparameters using the validation set. 4.3 EVALUATION METRICS Image reconstruction fidelity. We report peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index (SSIM) (Wang et al., 2004), and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) (Zhang et al., 2018a). PSNR quantifies pixel-level fidelity based on mean squared error, SSIM compares local luminance, contrast, and structure, and LPIPS measures perceptual distance in learned feature space. Vessel segmentation agreement. We apply the same fixed VSNet segmenter to every reconstructed volume and compare its HV and PV predictions with the reference annotations. Dice measures volumetric overlap, while clDice measures skeleton-based agreement (Shit et al., 2021). Three-dimensional vascular structure. To complement Dice and clDice, we further assess vascular fragmentation and the spatial alignment of vessel centerlines with the reference anatomy. We use 26-connectivity to compute connected components separately for HV and PV. For {HV, PV}, #CC counts components, and the largest-component fraction is Cmax,c/Pc, where Pc is the predicted foreground of class and Cmax,c its largest connected component. Mean centerline distance (MCD) measures the geometric discrepancy between predicted and reference vessel trajectories (Zhang et al., 2025). Nevertheless, VascuSR achieves the best LPIPS, which captures perceptual similarity in texture and local structure, and leads all methods across the Dice and clDice measures of anatomical fidelity. These results indicate that VascuSR focuses more on improving vascular structure recovery in SR images while preserving the backbones image reconstruction capability. detailed comparative analysis of VascuSR and ResShift+Dice/clDice across local appearance, vascular topology, and other aspects is provided in Appendix B. Additional results on vessel continuity and centerline accuracy are reported in Table 2. 4.5 THREE-DIMENSIONAL VASCULAR STRUCTURE Across MSD and HVM  (Table 2)  , VascuSR reduces component counts and increases largestcomponent fractions for both classes relative to ResShift. Bicubic has the lowest PV count, but its lower largest-component fraction illustrates why low count alone does not imply better continuity: under-segmentation can also reduce counts. On MSD, PV MCD decreases from 8.0877 mm with ResShift to 6.6351 mm, reduction of 18.0%. These results show that VascuSR reconstructs less fragmented vascular structures with centerlines that more closely follow the reference anatomy. Manual inspection of HVM annotations reveals isolated fragments and incomplete HV coverage at the hepatocaval junctions, where hepatic veins drain into the inferior vena cava. The resulting fragments 7 Preprint and separate major venous subtrees explain the elevated component counts and HV largest-component fraction of approximately 0.60. An ablation study of anatomical conditioning and iterative feedback is provided in Appendix A.2. It shows that VascuSR benefits from anatomical guidance and that Dice and clDice improve with feedback, largely stabilizing after two to three rounds. 4.6 QUALITATIVE ANALYSIS We further provide qualitative visualizations to examine local vascular changes that are not fully captured by aggregate scores. Modest changes in Dice can conceal clear local structural differences. In Figure 2, the two central PV portions appear separated in the ResShift reconstruction. After three feedback rounds, VascuSR improves their visible connection and recovers additional vessel contours visible in the HR reference. Figure 3 further shows three-dimensional vascular morphology. After three feedback rounds, the vascular trees are visibly more continuous, while several small isolated components present in the initial SR-derived segmentation are removed. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION AND DISCUSSION
sections.content: We introduced VascuSR, an iterative anatomy-aware diffusion framework for vascular CT superresolution that decouples three-dimensional vascular refinement from CT intensity reconstruction and connects them through anatomical conditioning. Across MSD Task08 and HVM, VascuSR improves Dice and clDice over the matched ResShift backbone while maintaining comparable image-level reconstruction quality. Connectivity and centerline analyses further show reduced fragmentation and closer agreement with reference vessel geometry. Further comparisons with joint optimization of image reconstruction and anatomical objectives support the benefits of our decoupled design in local image fidelity, vascular structure, and training efficiency. These findings support learning an anatomical prior in vascular label space and transferring it to SR through conditioning, while retaining HR-supervised reconstruction as the image objective. Limitations and Future Work. The current framework performs SR slice-wise and relies on fixed vessel segmenter and separately trained 3D refiner, which may limit volumetric consistency and allow errors to accumulate across feedback iterations. We also present exploratory results on coronary CTA in Appendix C, extending the evaluation beyond hepatic vessels. However, larger-scale evaluation across diverse vascular systems remains necessary. Future work will investigate fully volumetric and more tightly integrated reconstruction frameworks, adaptive or more efficient refinement, and broader evaluation across anatomies, acquisition settings, and downstream vascular-analysis tasks. sections.title: A APPENDIX
sections.content: A.1 TRAINING AND INFERENCE DETAILS Patient splits. Table 4 reports the patient-level dataset partitions. For MSD, 81 of the 243 training patients are used to train FlowSeg3D and the remaining 162 to train the joint SR/controller model. For HVM, the corresponding counts are 75 and 148 out of 223 training patients. The VSNet is trained on all patients of the training sets. Table 4: Patient-level dataset partitions. Dataset Training Validation Re-annotated MSD Task08 HVM 243 223 30 29 Test 30 29 Controller training conditions. During joint training of the SR backbone and anatomy controller, we sample anatomical conditions from three sources: raw VSNet labels from HR images, FlowSeg3Drefined labels from SR images, and an all-zero mask. The corresponding sampling probabilities are 0.35, 0.35, and 0.30 on MSD, and 0.425, 0.425, and 0.15 on HVM, respectively. SR training objective. The backbone and controller are jointly trained from scratch with the official ResShift objective. The VQ-f4 autoencoder remains frozen, and the LPIPS reference is its round-trip reconstruction of the HR target. SR optimization and inference. We use AdamW with learning rate of 5 105 and global batch size of 16, and use the checkpoint at 50,000 updates. Training and inference use the four-step ResShift diffusion process. Training is performed with DDP on four NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs. FlowSeg3D inputs and training. On both datasets, the velocity network is 3D U-Net with 24 base channels, trained on 128 128 96 patches with batch size 2 and an 80% probability of foreground-centered sampling. We use AdamW with learning rate 2 104, 500 warm-up iterations, and EMA decay 0.999, optimizing the velocity MSE in Equation 5. The noise amplitude in Equation 4 is σ = 1.0 during both training and inference on MSD and HVM. FlowSeg3D inference. The region of interest is the VSNet-predicted vessel bounding box expanded by 24 voxels. Velocity predictions use sliding windows with 50% overlap. We integrate = 8 independent-noise trajectories in parallel from τ = 1 to τ = 0 with ten Euler steps, keeping the probability condition fixed. After hard decoding, class frequencies are aggregated as in Equation 6. We retain frequencies strictly above 0.3 on MSD and 0.4 on HVM, corresponding to at least three and four votes out of eight, respectively. These thresholds are selected separately on the validation set of each dataset. If both classes pass, the higher frequency wins, with ties assigned to HV. 14 Preprint A.2 ABLATION STUDY: ITERATIVE ANATOMICAL FEEDBACK We examine how anatomical fidelity and image quality change over successive feedback rounds. On MSD  (Table 5)  , all five feedback rounds improve the reported Dice and clDice scores over ResShift. These metrics largely stabilize by round 3, with later rounds showing fluctuations rather than consistent gains. Image-quality metrics remain similar across feedback rounds. This indicates that VascuSRs anatomical gains depend on anatomical conditioning rather than increased model capacity alone. 15 Preprint A.3 ADDITIONAL QUALITATIVE RESULTS Figure 4: Additional qualitative comparison on held-out MSD case 416 at axial slice = 114. Columns show LR, ResShift, VascuSR after three feedback rounds, and the HR reference (GT). The upper row shows intensity crops; the lower row adds vascular contours to the reconstructed and HR images. Red and blue denote HV and PV, respectively. In Figure 4, low-contrast, approximately circular HV cross-section in the lower-right region is only weakly and irregularly delineated by ResShift. Anatomical feedback makes its boundary more regular and the predicted contour closer to the manual annotation. 16 Preprint (a) (b) Figure 5: Additional qualitative comparison on held-out HVM case 109 at axial slices (a) = 179 and (b) = 204. Columns show LR, ResShift, VascuSR after two feedback rounds, and the HR reference (GT). The upper row of each panel shows intensity crops; the lower row adds vascular contours to the reconstructed and HR images. Red and blue denote HV and PV, respectively; HR contours are manual annotations. In panel (a), the central HV cross-section appears rounded in ResShift, whereas VascuSR recovers more angular shape that more closely resembles the HR reference. In panel (b), the elongated HV and PV structures near the center appear interrupted in ResShift and become more continuous with VascuSR. 17 Preprint Figure 6: Three-dimensional qualitative comparison on four held-out HVM cases. Columns show the initial SR segmentation, round-2 SR segmentation, and segmentation of the HR reference. Red and blue denote HV and PV, respectively. 18 Preprint WHY ANATOMICAL CONDITIONING RATHER THAN SEGMENTATION-LOSS FINE-TUNING? VascuSR starts from two requirements for vascular CT super-resolution: reconstruct CT images that are faithful to the HR reference while preserving vascular anatomical plausibility. diffusion reconstruction objective addresses the first requirement, but spatially averaged image agreement alone does not ensure that the reconstructed vasculature is anatomically plausible. 3D vessel representation is therefore useful source of supervision: it captures continuity and branching across slices and, with more fine-grained segmentation, can also provide vessel categories. The design question is how to turn this structural supervision into learning signal, and which architecture should carry it. The most direct approach is to add Dice and soft-clDice to the SR objective and fine-tune the image generator through frozen segmenter. This approach works: on MSD it improves Dice and clDice over ResShift  (Table 1)  . To explain why we use anatomical conditioning rather than direct fine-tuning, we first compare the two training strategies, then examine the limitations of this fine-tuning baseline and the advantages of VascuSR in image fidelity in the vessel neighborhood, vascular structure, and training cost. B.1 TWO WAYS TO INTRODUCE ANATOMICAL SUPERVISION We seek an SR image with both image fidelity and anatomically plausible vessels. These requirements can be expressed by the conceptual objective min Limage(Y ; X) (cid:124) (cid:123)(cid:122) (cid:125) image fidelity +λ Φ(T (Y )) (cid:123)(cid:122) (cid:125) (cid:124) anatomical plausibility . (10) Here is the LR input, extracts the vascular representation from , and Φ penalizes anatomically implausible structure. The two strategies below differ in how they address these image and anatomy requirements. Direct fine-tuning with Dice and soft-clDice. Fine-tuning implements the two requirements through the joint objective min ω Limage(Yω; X) + λ [LDice(T (Yω), ) + α Lsoft-clDice(T (Yω), )] . (11) Here Yω is the SR output, is the task-specific reference segmentation, and ω denotes the generator parameters. The image and anatomy losses update the same generator, with frozen. We evaluate checkpoints after 1,200 optimizer updates on MSD and 2,000 optimizer updates on HVM, using learning rates of 105 and 5 106, respectively. In both settings, α is gradually increased from 0 to 0.5. Small learning rates are used to preserve the pretrained reconstruction behavior, while the warm-up introduces skeleton supervision gradually. Implicit anatomical regularization through conditioning. VascuSR addresses Equation 10 through two separately supervised tasks: the SR model learns image fidelity from HR, while the refiner learns vascular correction toward the manual reference through its flow loss (Equation 5). In this supervised interpretation, write the anatomical penalty as Φ(V ) = d(V, ), where is metric on the shared vascular representation, such as voxelwise L1. For the refined condition (cid:101)V = Rψ(T (Y0)) and its conditioned reconstruction Y1. Φ(T (Y1)) = d(T (Y1), ) (cid:125) (cid:123)(cid:122) (cid:124) final vascular error d( (cid:101)V , ) (cid:124) (cid:123)(cid:122) (cid:125) refinement error , + d(T (Y1), (cid:101)V ) (cid:125) (cid:123)(cid:122) transfer error (cid:124) (12) Thus, the final vascular error is the anatomical penalty in Equation 10. When conditioning keeps the transfer error small, reducing refinement error tightens the bound on that penalty. Image reconstruction and vascular refinement therefore address the two terms through separate supervised objectives, with conditioning linking them. 19 Preprint B.2 IMAGE FIDELITY NEAR VESSELS We assess whether improved vascular segmentation is accompanied by faithful CT reconstruction near vessels. Table 7 compares final SR images with HR within 3 mm dilation of the manual HV/PV union. SSIM and spatial LPIPS are sampled within the ROI from maps computed on full, unmasked slices. Table 7: Image quality within the 3 mm vessel ROI on the MSD test set. Values are patient-macro means; PSNR is in dB. This comparison uses VascuSR R3. Method ROI PSNR ROI SSIM ROI spatial-LPIPS ResShift ResShift+Dice/clDice VascuSR, round 3 34.5933 33.0302 34.4383 0.815880 0.786745 0.815435 0.155418 0.160075 0. VascuSR R3 improves all three ROI image-quality metrics over fine-tuning. For complementary assessment of absolute CT intensity, Table 8 reports MAE, RMSE, and signed bias against native HR within 3 mm dilation of the manual HV/PV union. For ROI voxels, let ei be the SR intensity minus the HR intensity at voxel i. Then MAE = 1 (cid:80) , and signed bias = 1 ei, RMSE = (cid:112)N 1 (cid:80) i=1 ei. e2 (cid:80)N Table 8: Image fidelity within the 3 mm vessel ROI on the MSD test set. Values are in HU; positive bias indicates overestimated intensity. Method MAE RMSE Signed bias ( 0) ResShift VascuSR, round 3 ResShift+Dice/clDice 21.97 22.21 26. 29.61 29.86 34.40 +1.95 +4.14 +12.59 Tables 7 and 8 show that VascuSR largely preserves ResShifts regional image quality (PSNR, SSIM, and spatial LPIPS) and image fidelity (MAE, RMSE, and signed bias), with modest degradation in some measures. We consider this an acceptable trade-off for pursuing anatomical plausibility alongside image fidelity, supported by the structural improvements in Tables 1 and 5. In contrast, ResShift+Dice/clDice worsens all six regional measures, indicating that direct fine-tuning improves Dice and clDice at the expense of substantially reduced local vascular image fidelity. B.3 CROSS-SEGMENTER EVALUATION AND LOCAL APPEARANCE On the MSD test set, ResShift+Dice/clDice raises VSNet HV Dice from ResShifts 0.6526 to 0.7010, close to VascuSR R3 at 0.7072 (Tables 1 and 5). To test whether this gain extends beyond VSNet, we evaluate the same reconstructions with frozen TotalSegmentator (TS 2.13.0) (Wasserthal et al., 2023). Fine-tuning falls below ResShift, whereas VascuSR R3 improves by 2.71 percentage points  (Table 9)  . Low absolute scores may partly reflect coverage mismatch: the manual GT includes large-caliber extrahepatic venous segments not captured by these TS predictions. Table 9: TS vessel Dice on the MSD test set. Method TS vessel Dice ResShift VascuSR, round 3 ResShift+Dice/clDice .2912 .3183 .2803 20 Preprint Figure 7 examines the corresponding image appearance on MSD case 416. VascuSR restores the visible connection between the two vessel portions in the central PV, whereas fine-tuning does not visibly improve this connection. In the fine-tuned CT, the vessel portions are conspicuously bright, while the predicted blue contour still spans their connection. segmentation contour can therefore look plausible even where the underlying intensity profile appears discontinuous. Figure 7: Qualitative comparison on MSD case 416, axial slice = 094. Columns show LR, ResShift, VascuSR after three feedback rounds, ResShift+Dice/clDice, and the HR reference. The upper row shows CT images; the lower row adds vascular contours, with HV in red and PV in blue. HR contours are manual annotations. The brightening of vessel regions is also supported by quantitative intensity measurements: ResShift+Dice/clDice has 3 mm ROI signed bias of +12.59 HU, compared with +1.95 HU for ResShift and +4.14 HU for VascuSR R3  (Table 8)  . When evaluated with TS, fine-tuning shows no Dice improvement and instead scores slightly below ResShift  (Table 9)  . Together with vessel brightening and the qualitative intensitycontour mismatch (Figure 7), this suggests that the model may have learned segmenter-specific appearance shortcut, making vessels easier for VSNet to segment without improving their image fidelity. Its explicit Dice/clDice loss (Equation 11) directly rewards such segmentation gains. VascuSR instead learns structural correction in vascular label space and transfers it through anatomical conditioning (Equation 12), while retaining HR-supervised reconstruction as the image generators training objective. Without backpropagating Dice loss through the generator, this design removes the direct Dice-based incentive to exploit segmenters response and encourages the generator to use the refined anatomical condition to improve vascular topology and reconstruction. B.4 VASCULAR TOPOLOGY Tables 10 and 11 compare vascular continuity and centerline accuracy on the same MSD test set. Connectivity uses 3D 26-neighborhoods. Table 10: MSD vascular continuity for the three relevant methods, reproduced from Table 2. Method #CC Largest-CC frac #CC Largest-CC frac HV PV ResShift ResShift+Dice/clDice VascuSR, round 3 31.0 39.6 22.7 26.0 30.4 22.4 .8843 .8249 . .9077 .8936 .9382 21 Preprint Table 11: Class-wise MSD MCD values (mm) from Table 2, with their HV/PV mean additionally reported. Method ResShift VascuSR, round 3 ResShift+Dice/clDice HV 6.0457 5.2311 5.6521 PV 8.0877 6.6351 7.5368 HV/PV mean 7.0667 5.9331 6. VascuSR improves both connectivity measures over ResShift+Dice/clDice, which even produces more components than ResShift; MCD also favors VascuSR on both MSD and HVM (Tables 11 and 2). One possible contributor to the poorer connectivity is the gap between soft supervision and binary structure. Soft-clDice encourages skeleton continuity using differentiable soft-skeleton approximation (Shit et al., 2021). Optimizing this relaxed objective does not directly enforce every connection in the thresholded mask, so local breaks can remain after binarization. Together, the connectivity and MCD results highlight limitation of direct fine-tuning: anatomy is specified through manually selected differentiable penalties (Equation 11). These can favor the chosen scores while prompting repeated additions of constraints and weight tuning, without fully capturing what makes vascular structure anatomically plausible. VascuSR instead decouples vascular refinement from CT intensity reconstruction, removing organ texture and other high-frequency image details from the structural learning task. In this simpler 3D label space, the lightweight refiner uses single conditional rectified-flow velocity-matching loss to learn the mapping from noisy imperfect predictions to GT (Equation 5). It thereby learns vascular spatial dependencies and implicitly models conditional distribution of plausible vessel structures from paired annotations, without additional Dice, clDice, or other morphology-specific losses. The refinementconditioning loop transfers this learned anatomical prior to SR while retaining HR reconstruction as the image objective (Equation 12). B.5 COMPUTATIONAL CONSEQUENCES OF DECOUPLING Direct fine-tuning is also computationally expensive. Because the segmenter operates in 3D, each update must generate multiple SR slices, assemble them into volume, compute Dice and soft-clDice from the segmentation, and backpropagate through the segmenter and SR generator. This repeated computation makes fine-tuning slow in practice. Table 12: Training costs on HVM, excluding validation. The refiner is trained to the selected 50k checkpoint; ResShift+Dice/clDice is trained for 2,000 effective optimizer updates. For VascuSR, we report the training cost of the 3D vascular refiner. Training stage Wall time (h) GPU-hours VascuSR refiner ResShift+Dice/clDice 9.80 29.33 24.60 94. Table 12 shows that VascuSRs vascular refiner requires less training time and fewer GPU-hours than direct fine-tuning. Restricting refinement to vascular representation space simplifies the learning task, allowing lightweight generative refiner to learn effective structural correction with substantially less training time than direct fine-tuning. In addition, training the ResShift backbone jointly with the anatomy controller takes approximately the same time as training the backbone alone. 22 Preprint

sections.title: C EXTENSION TO CORONARY CTA ON IMAGECAS
sections.content: Dataset and evaluation scope. We extend our evaluation beyond hepatic vessels to ImageCAS, coronary CT angiography dataset (Zeng et al., 2023). We use 300-case subset with 200 training, 50 validation, and 50 test cases. Coronary segmenter. We initialize from the pretrained Dataset509 coronary model in TotalSegmentator 2.13 (Wasserthal et al., 2023) and fine-tune the entire network on the 200 training HR CT volumes and their manual binary coronary annotations. Training uses 1283 patches, batch size 2, and SGD with an initial learning rate of 0.001, momentum 0.99, Nesterov acceleration, weight decay 3 105, and polynomial learning-rate decay. Table 13: Coronary CTA results on the ImageCAS test set. Bold marks the best SR result in each column. Method RCAN SwinIR ResShift VascuSR (Round 3) HR reference Dice 0.7699 0.7702 0.7658 0.7763 0.8033 clDice PSNR (dB) SSIM 0.8432 0.8409 0.8376 0.8530 0.8610 31.29 31.41 29.94 29.84 0.8079 0.8096 0.7647 0.7629 1. Results and interpretation. Table 13 shows that VascuSR achieves the highest Dice and clDice among the evaluated SR methods. The absolute Dice and clDice gains over ResShift in Table 13 are modest, which may be caused by the fact that coronary vessel configurations are less complex than those in the hepatic setting, leaving less room for anatomical correction. Moreover, ResShift already performs close to the HR segmentation reference. VascuSR closes 28.0% of the ResShift-to-HR gap in Dice and 65.8% of that gap in clDice.
